name: The Signature Delta-V Ladder
title: The Signature Delta-V Ladder
description: The Signature Delta-V Ladder is JAH's original teaching framework for mission design. Every maneuver a spacecraft ever performs is sorted into one of three rungs: BURN (change your velocity), COAST (spend time, spend no propellant), CAPTURE (arrive somewhere and stay). The doctrine is simple: a mission is a ladder of rungs, and you never climb a rung you cannot count. It turns the overwhelming algebra of astrodynamics into a checklist a beginner can audit and an expert can trust.
how_it_works: You decompose any mission into an ordered list of velocity changes, each tagged with its rung. BURN rungs carry a magnitude in km/s and a propulsion assumption; COAST rungs carry a duration and a navigation check; CAPTURE rungs carry an arrival velocity and a target orbit. You sum the BURN rungs for the mission delta-v, add the Signature margin doctrine on top, and the ladder becomes your budget. If a rung cannot be quantified, the mission is not designed yet — that is the framework's whole discipline, and its whole value.
key_points: Three rungs only: burn, coast, capture
Every burn is a counted number before it is a maneuver
Capture-first ordering: the arrival is designed before the departure
The ladder doubles as the mission's delta-v budget and audit trail
requirements: A mission concept with at least a departure and an arrival; a delta-v estimate for each burn rung.
standards: Signature original framework. Burn magnitudes use standard vis-viva and rocket-equation inputs where quantified; the three-rung ladder structure is JAH's original doctrine.
citations: Builds on the vis-viva equation and Tsiolkovsky (1903) for burn-magnitude inputs

name: The Perfect Burn Principle
title: The Perfect Burn Principle
description: The Perfect Burn Principle is JAH's original impulse-timing doctrine. It states that every burn has a perfect instant — the point in the orbit where that velocity change buys the most — and every second of burn duration away from that instant is tax paid to reality. The principle does not pretend burns are instantaneous; it demands you know exactly what the instant would have bought, so you can measure what the finite burn cost. That measurement is where real mission design begins.
how_it_works: You compute the impulsive delta-v first, always — that is the perfect-burn reference. Then you spread the burn over its real duration and estimate finite-burn efficiency: a tangential burn spread over an orbital arc of fraction f keeps roughly sin(pi*f)/(pi*f) of its effectiveness, so the required delta-v grows by the inverse of that factor. The doctrine's rule of thumb: if the finite-burn tax exceeds ten percent, split the burn across multiple perigee passes or get a bigger engine — never just silently accept the tax.
key_points: The impulsive burn is the reference; the real burn is measured against it
Finite-burn tax grows with burn arc: eta = sin(pi*f)/(pi*f)
Tax above 10% means re-architect: split the burn or upsize thrust
Applies to every chemical burn; low-thrust spirals live under the Spiral Doctrine instead
requirements: An impulsive delta-v value and an estimate of burn duration as a fraction of the orbital period.
standards: Signature original doctrine. The finite-burn efficiency relation is a classical approximation used here as a Signature design input.
citations: Builds on classical impulsive-maneuver theory; finite-burn efficiency approximation from standard astrodynamics

name: Signature Mass-Fraction Thinking
title: Signature Mass-Fraction Thinking
description: Signature mass-fraction thinking is JAH's original compounding doctrine: fuel carries fuel, so every kilogram of propellant must also push the propellant that pushes it. Beginners think of propellant as something you buy; this doctrine teaches you to think of it as something you also have to carry. The worked rule: doubling your delta-v more than doubles your propellant — it multiplies it exponentially through the rocket equation. Once you feel that compounding in your gut, you design like a mission architect instead of a shopper.
how_it_works: You start from the payload you must deliver and work backward through Tsiolkovsky's equation: mass ratio = e^(dv/(Isp*g0)). Given a structural fraction, you solve for the propellant that the dry mass demands, then check the ratio — if propellant exceeds about 85% of the stack, the doctrine flags the design as fragile and sends you to staging (the Three-Tank Rule) or refueling (the depot doctrine). The thinking is always backward from the payload, never forward from the tank.
key_points: Fuel carries fuel: propellant mass compounds exponentially with delta-v
Design backward from the payload, never forward from the tank
Propellant above ~85% of stack mass flags a fragile design
The rocket equation is the doctrine's calculator; the doctrine is how you read its answer
requirements: A delta-v requirement, an engine specific impulse, a payload mass, and a structural fraction estimate.
standards: Signature original doctrine. The rocket equation itself is Tsiolkovsky (1903); the backward-design method and fragility flag are JAH's original framework.
citations: Builds on Tsiolkovsky (1903), the rocket equation

# JAH-DVS-000003 -- Signature mass-fraction thinking: "fuel carries fuel" calculator
import math
g0 = 9.80665
isp = 320.0        # s, hypergolic upper stage
dv = 1000.0        # m/s, worked example: 1 km/s maneuver

print("  Deliver %d kg through %.1f km/s at Isp %d s" % (payload, dv / 1000, isp))
print("  Mass ratio required: %.3f" % mr)
print("  Dry mass:            %8.1f kg" % dry)
print("  Propellant needed:   %8.1f kg  <- the fuel that carries the fuel" % prop)
print("  Propellant fraction: %5.1f%% of stack" % (prop / m0 * 100))
print("  Doctrine flag:       %s" % ("FRAGILE -- stage it or depot it" if prop / m0 > 0.85 else "SOUND -- single burn acceptable"))

name: The Three-Tank Rule
title: The Three-Tank Rule
description: The Three-Tank Rule is JAH's original staging doctrine: never carry an empty tank through a burn you could have dropped it before. The framework pictures every vehicle as three tanks — the one you burn, the one you drop, the one you keep — and sizes them so each stage delivers a roughly equal share of the mission delta-v. Equal shares are the doctrine's signature heuristic: they keep every stage in its efficient zone and no stage becomes a dead-weight passenger. Staging is not complexity for its own sake; it is refusing to pay compounding tax on empty metal.
how_it_works: You split the total delta-v into stage shares, aiming for near-equal per-stage delta-v, and you drop each stage's dry structure the moment its propellant is spent. The calculator compares a single-stage stack against a two-stage stack with identical payload and propellant: the staged vehicle always wins because the second burn no longer pushes the first stage's empty tanks. The doctrine's audit question for any design: point at every kilogram of structure and name the burn that still needs it — if you cannot, it should have been dropped already.
key_points: Three tanks: the one you burn, the one you drop, the one you keep
Size stages for roughly equal delta-v shares
Drop dry structure the instant its propellant is spent
Audit every structural kilogram: name the burn that still needs it
requirements: A total delta-v requirement, payload mass, per-stage structural masses, and engine Isp.
standards: Signature original doctrine. Staging mathematics via Tsiolkovsky (1903); the three-tank framing and equal-share heuristic are JAH original.
citations: Builds on Tsiolkovsky (1903) applied per stage

name: Reading Velocity Like a Map
title: Reading Velocity Like a Map
description: Reading velocity like a map is JAH's original spatial-intuition method for maneuver design. The doctrine: velocity is a map, the orbit is the territory, and every direction you can push is a direction on that map — prograde grows the orbit, retrograde shrinks it, normal tilts the plane, radial rotates the line of apsides. Students who learn this stop memorizing formulas and start seeing: a retrograde burn at apogee is obviously how you lower perigee, because you can watch the map fold. Intuition first, vis-viva second, and the numbers always agree with the picture.
how_it_works: You decompose any planned burn into the map's four compass directions and read the effect before computing it: prograde/retrograde change energy (orbit size), radial changes orientation, normal changes inclination. Then you verify with vis-viva: a retrograde burn of 0.10 km/s from a 400 km circular orbit lowers perigee by a computable amount, and the map told you the direction before the equation told you the number. The method's discipline is that the picture and the math must agree — if they disagree, you misread the map, and you re-read before you burn.
key_points: Four compass directions: prograde, retrograde, normal, radial
Prograde/retrograde change energy; normal changes plane; radial rotates apsides
Read the direction from the map first, then compute the magnitude
Picture and math must agree before any burn is trusted
requirements: A starting orbit (altitude or elements) and a planned burn vector.
standards: Signature original teaching method. Orbital mechanics via the vis-viva equation; the four-direction map framing is JAH original.
citations: Builds on the vis-viva equation (standard orbital mechanics)

name: The Patience Burn
title: The Patience Burn
description: The Patience Burn is JAH's original low-thrust philosophy: thrust is a rumor, time is the engine. Where the Perfect Burn Principle worships the instant, the Patience Burn worships the long arc — a whisper of thrust sustained for months can deliver the delta-v of a chemical stage while sipping propellant at ion-engine specific impulses of 3000 seconds and more. The doctrine's core judgment call: crew and narrow windows demand impulse; cargo, pre-positioning, and station infrastructure reward patience. Choosing wrong — rushing cargo or creeping crew — is the classic mission-design sin this framework exists to prevent.
how_it_works: You trade thrust against time with one relation: burn time equals delta-v divided by acceleration. A 0.2-newton ion thruster pushing a 2000 kg spacecraft accelerates at one ten-thousandth of a g, so a 7.8 km/s spiral out of low Earth orbit takes on the order of 890 days — but the propellant mass collapses by an order of magnitude versus chemical. The framework's audit: if the cargo can wait, patience buys you mass; if it cannot, patience is just lateness with better fuel economy. The calculator makes the trade visible in days and kilograms.
key_points: Thrust is a rumor; time is the engine
Burn time = delta-v / acceleration: the whole trade in one relation
Patience buys propellant mass at the price of calendar time
Crew and windows demand impulse; cargo rewards patience
requirements: A delta-v requirement, a thrust level, a spacecraft mass, and a schedule constraint.
standards: Signature original philosophy. Low-thrust spiral approximation (delta-v near the circular-orbit velocity difference) and the rocket equation; the patience-vs-impulse doctrine is JAH original.
citations: Builds on Tsiolkovsky (1903); ion Isp ~3000-4000 s is standard published performance

g0 = 9.80665

print("  Spiral time:  %7.1f days (time is the engine)" % days)
print("  Propellant if ion (Isp %d s):   %7.1f kg" % (isp_ion, prop_ion))
print("  Propellant if chemical (Isp %d s): %7.1f kg" % (isp_chem, prop_chem))
print("  Patience buys: %7.1f kg of mass for %6.0f days of calendar" % (prop_chem - prop_ion, days))
print("  Doctrine: cargo waits, crew does not.")

name: Signature Gravity-Turn Doctrine
title: Signature Gravity-Turn Doctrine
description: The Signature gravity-turn doctrine is JAH's original ascent framework: fly the turn, don't fight it. A rocket climbing out of the atmosphere pitches over early and lets gravity bend its trajectory toward horizontal, so that by the time the air is gone the vehicle is already flying sideways — the cheapest possible path to orbital velocity. The doctrine's signature budget rule: reaching low Earth orbit costs about 9.3 to 9.8 km/s of delta-v, of which only 7.8 is orbital velocity and the rest is tax — gravity loss, drag loss, steering loss. Beginners budget 7.8 and run dry; the doctrine budgets the tax first.
how_it_works: You build the ascent budget as ideal velocity plus losses: 7.8 km/s circular velocity, plus gravity loss (fighting g while climbing, typically ~1.0-1.5 km/s), plus drag loss (~0.1-0.2 km/s), plus steering loss for the pitch program (~0.1 km/s). The gravity turn itself minimizes steering loss — the trajectory bends under gravity alone once the initial pitch-over is done. The calculator assembles the budget from loss estimates and shows, line by line, where the extra ~1.5-2.0 km/s beyond orbital velocity goes, so no ascent plan ever pretends the tax does not exist.
key_points: Fly the turn, don't fight it: pitch over early, let gravity bend the path
LEO costs ~9.3-9.8 km/s; only 7.8 is orbital velocity, the rest is tax
Budget gravity loss + drag loss + steering loss as explicit line items
The gravity turn minimizes steering loss by design
requirements: A target orbit altitude and estimates of gravity, drag, and steering losses (or vehicle T/W to derive them).
standards: Signature original doctrine. Loss magnitudes are standard published ranges; the fly-the-turn framing and tax-first budgeting are JAH original.
citations: Builds on standard launch-vehicle ascent analysis; LEO ~7.8 km/s circular, ~9.3-10 km/s surface-to-LEO are standard figures

name: The Capture-First Rule
title: The Capture-First Rule
description: The Capture-First Rule is JAH's original arrival-planning doctrine: plan the capture burn before the departure burn. Most failed mission concepts die at arrival — they can afford to leave, but they cannot afford to stay, so the spacecraft sails past its destination as the most expensive flyby in history. The rule inverts the design order: compute the capture delta-v from the arrival velocity first, prove you can afford to stop, and only then design the departure. A mission you cannot capture is not a mission; it is a very fast postcard.
how_it_works: You start from the arrival hyperbolic excess velocity (v-infinity) at the destination and the target capture orbit. The periapsis velocity of the arrival hyperbola is sqrt(v_inf^2 + v_esc^2), and the capture burn is that minus the target orbit's circular velocity. The calculator runs this for a Mars arrival: with a typical 2.6 km/s v-infinity, capturing into a 500 km Mars orbit costs about 2.1 km/s — a number that must sit in the ledger before a single departure calculation is trusted. If the capture is unaffordable, the doctrine sends you to aerocapture studies or a different window, not to wishful thinking.
key_points: Design the arrival before the departure
Capture delta-v = arrival-hyperbola periapsis velocity minus target circular velocity
A mission you cannot capture is a flyby, not a mission
Unaffordable capture means a new window or aerocapture — never wishful thinking
requirements: An arrival v-infinity, the destination body's gravitational parameter, and a target capture orbit.
standards: Signature original doctrine. Patched-conic arrival mathematics is standard; the capture-first design ordering is JAH original.
citations: Builds on standard patched-conic arrival analysis

Running total must close against vehicle capability

name: The Margin Doctrine
title: The Margin Doctrine
description: The Margin Doctrine is JAH's original reserve-delta-v framework: margin is not pessimism, it is the part of the mission that has already gone wrong. The doctrine sets three reserve rules of thumb — ten percent on every computed burn, a flat 100 m/s navigation reserve for the things nobody modeled, and one extra correction burn sized at five percent of the largest maneuver for the anomaly nobody predicted. Missions designed without margin are designed for a universe that does not exist; the doctrine designs for the one that does, where engines underperform, navigation errs, and windows slip.
how_it_works: You apply the three rules mechanically to the ledger: each burn row grows by ten percent, the flat 100 m/s reserve is added once at the mission level, and the contingency correction — five percent of the largest single burn — is appended as its own ledger row so it is visible and auditable. The calculator runs the doctrine on a sample interplanetary ledger and shows the reserve stack explicitly: margin is a line item, not a hope, and anyone reviewing the design can see exactly how much trouble the mission is prepared to survive. Spending margin in design is cheap; spending it in flight is impossible.
key_points: 10% on every computed burn, no exceptions
Flat 100 m/s navigation reserve at mission level
One contingency correction: 5% of the largest single burn
Margin is a line item, not a hope
requirements: A ledger of computed burns (magnitudes in km/s).

name: Signature Hohmann-Plus Framework
title: Signature Hohmann-Plus Framework
description: The Signature Hohmann-plus framework is JAH's original refinement layer on the classical Hohmann transfer.
